Many ancient manuscripts include the phrase the Son of God. A few ancient manuscripts do not include these words.
1:2: Here, Isaiah the prophet represents the book written by Isaiah.
Here, the phrase before your face means before or in front of the person.
Here the author of the quotation speaks of helping people to get ready for the coming of the Messiah as if it were preparing the way or road for the Messiah.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

Here the author of the quotation speaks as if people should build or maintain roads for the Lord to travel on as he comes to visit his people. He means that people need to be living and acting in proper ways when the Lord appears to his people.
1:4: Here, the phrase translated as the one baptizing could be: (1) a description of what John did, in parallel with the word preaching; (2) a title (“the Baptist”) that people called John.
Here Mark implies that John was preaching that people should undergo a baptism of repentance.
1:5: πᾶσα ἡ Ἰουδαία χώρα καὶ οἱ Ἱεροσολυμεῖται πάντες
Mark twice writes all as a generalization for emphasis.
Here, the phrase all the Judea region represents the people who live in that area.
Here it is the people who are confessing, not John.

Here Mark implies that John wore clothes made from camel hair.

1:7: Here John speaks as if someone is walking behind him. He means that soon someone will continue what he has started doing.

λῦσαι τὸν ἱμάντα τῶν ὑποδημάτων αὐτοῦ

1:15: When time has been fulfilled, that means that it is now the moment that God has appointed for something to happen.
Here Mark uses this phrase in the sense of near in time.

Here Jesus speaks of preaching the gospel and helping people believe in Jesus as if it were fishing. 1:26: Here Mark is referring to a fit or seizure in which a person cannot control his or her body, which shakes violently.

Here Jesus means that the man should show himself to the priest and offer the gift to prove or provide testimony that he had been healed.
1:45: κηρύσσειν πολλὰ καὶ διαφημίζειν τὸν λόγον

Here Mark implies that this house was Jesus’ home while he was in Capernaum. This house could belong to: (1) Simon and Andrew, since he stayed at their house previously (see 1:29); (2) Jesus and his relatives, who may have moved to Capernaum.
2:2: Here, the clause it could no longer receive means that the house was so full that no one else could fit inside.
Here Mark means that there were so many people even outside the house that no one could get near the door.
Mark is using the term word to mean the gospel, that Jesus preached using words.

In the region where Jesus lived, houses usually had flat roofs that could be reached by staircases on the outside of the houses. These roofs were usually made of wooden beams, branches, and packed dirt or clay. Here Mark describes how these people dug through the branches and clay to create a hole in the roof through which they could lower the paralytic on his mat.
Here Mark implies that they first climbed up onto the roof before they removed it.
A mat was a portable bed that could also be used to transport a person.
2:5: Here Mark implies that Jesus recognized that the friends of this paralyzed man strongly believed that he could heal him. Their actions proved that.
Here Jesus calls the paralytic Child to indicate that he cares for him. The word also implies that the paralytic was younger than Jesus. The paralytic was not actually Jesus’ son.
2:6: In Mark’s culture, hearts are the places where humans think and feel.
2:7: The scribes are using the question form to show that they disapprove of how Jesus was speaking.
The scribes are using the question form to indicate that they are confident that only God can forgive sins.
2:8: ἐπιγνοὺς ὁ Ἰησοῦς τῷ πνεύματι αὐτοῦ
Here Mark implies that Jesus knew what the scribes were thinking even though they did not say it out loud.
Here, the word spirit refers to inner parts of Jesus, the parts where he thought and willed.
τί ταῦτα διαλογίζεσθε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν
Jesus is using the question form to rebuke the scribes.

He could mean: (1) that saying Your sins are forgiven is easier than saying Get up and take up your mat and walk. This is because it is easy to show that someone is lying when they try to heal a paralytic, but it is not easy to show that someone is lying when they claim to forgive sins; (2) that both things are equally easy to say.
2:10: Here Jesus for the first time in Mark uses the title Son of Man to refer to himself. He is using the title to refer to himself, a human, and also to implicitly identify himself with the important and powerful figure named “the son of man” in the Old Testament book of Daniel (see Daniel 7:13–14). See the book introduction for more information about this title.
2:12: ἠγέρθη, καὶ εὐθὺς ἄρας τὸν κράβαττον, ἐξῆλθεν
The implication is that the man was able to get up because Jesus had healed him.
2:14: Here Mark means that Levi worked as a tax collector.

In Jesus’ culture, people would usually recline, or lay on one side, when they were eating.
Here, the phrase they were following him indicates that these people were traveling with Jesus and were his disciple.

The scribes of the Pharisees are using the question form to criticize what Jesus is doing.

Jesus is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete.
Here, the word come refers to Jesus entering this world as a human to do what God called him to do.

2:19: Jesus is using the question form to teach the people who asked him the question.

2:20: Here Jesus is using the word days to refer to a particular time.

Here Jesus refers to the practice of patching a hole or tear in a garment by sewing or attaching a patch to the garment to cover the hole or tear.

Here Jesus implies that the patch will tear away when the garment is washed, because the patch will shrink and rip the old garment.

These were bags made out of animal skins. They were used for holding wine.
Jesus is using a hypothetical situation to teach.
Here Jesus implies that the new wine, when it ferments, will expand and burst the wineskins, which are old and so no longer able to stretch.
2:23: Here Mark uses the phrase on the Sabbaths to indicate that this event occurred on one specific Sabbath day.
Mark is referring to Jesus to represent both Jesus and his disciples, who traveled with Jesus.
The word grainfields refers to places where grain is grown and harvested. This grain is usually ground and made into bread.
Here, the phrase to make a way means that the disciples were traveling or walking along.
Here Mark implies that the disciples ate the heads of grain after picking them.
The heads are the topmost part of the grain plant, which is a kind of tall grass. The heads hold the mature grain or seeds of the plant, which are the parts that people eat.

ποιοῦσιν τοῖς Σάββασιν ὃ οὐκ ἔξεστιν

2:25: Here Jesus is implying that David did not have everything that he needed, especially food.

3:3: Here, the implication is that Jesus wanted this man to stand where everyone could see him.

Here, the phrase save a life refers to preventing a person from dying.
3:5: Here, Jesus is speaking of the Pharisees’ heart as if it were characterized by hardness. He means that the Pharisees are stubborn and refuse to listen and learn.

μετὰ τῶν Ἡρῳδιανῶν συμβούλιον ἐποίουν κατ’ αὐτοῦ
Here, the phrase were making counsel with the Herodians against him indicates that the Pharisees were working together with the Herodians to figure out ways to harm Jesus.
3:8: Here, the phrase beyond the Jordan refers to regions to the east of the Jordan River.

Son of God is an important title for Jesus that describes his relationship with God the Father.

14:41: Here Mark implies that Jesus went away and prayed and then returned to the disciples the third time.

This sentence could be: (1) a rhetorical question that Jesus uses to rebuke the disciples. In this case, Jesus is disappointed that the disciples continue to sleep; (2) a command to continue to sleep and rest. In this case, Jesus means that the time when they were supposed to be alert is over, and they might as well sleep and rest now.
Jesus is using the question form to rebuke Peter, James, and John.
The terms sleeping and resting mean similar things. Jesus is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here Jesus implies that the disciples have slept enough, and they should wake up and be ready to act.
Here, the word hour refers to a specific moment in time.
Here, Jesus implies that the hour is the time when he will suffer.
The term hands represents power and control. See how expressed the similar idea in 9:31.
14:43: A “club” is a hard piece of wood that a person uses to hit people.
14:44: To help his readers understand what happens next, Mark provides this background information about how Judas had arranged his betrayal of Jesus with the Jewish leaders. Here Mark uses the word Now to introduce the background information which he gives in the rest of this verse.
Here Mark is referring to an action by which one person communicates to others. More specifically, Judas arranged with the crowd an action that would communicate to them which person was Jesus.
In Jesus’ culture, close friends would greet each other with a kiss. In some cultures, a kiss as a greeting is appropriate, but in other cultures it is not appropriate.
14:45: In Jesus’ culture, close friends would greet each other with a kiss.
14:46: The clauses they laid their hands on {him} and seized him mean similar things. Mark is using the two clauses together for emphasis.
Here, they laid their hands on {him} means that they grabbed and restrained Jesus.
14:48: Here, the word answering indicates that Jesus was responding to what had happened. He was not answering a question.
Jesus is using the question form to rebuke the people who were arresting him for how they were acting.
Jesus is saying that the crowds are acting like he is a dangerous robber because they have come to arrest him with many weapons.
14:49: Here Mark means that Jesus was teaching in the temple area. He does not mean that Jesus was in the most sacred parts of the temple building.
14:51: The term linen refers to a high-quality cloth made from the fibers of the flax plant.
Here Mark implies that the young man was not wearing anything except for the linen garment.
Here Mark implies that the men who arrested Jesus seized this young man by his garment.
14:52: Here Mark implies that the young man, when the crowd seized his garment to arrest him, slipped out of it and left it behind.
14:53: Here, the high priest represents the house where the high priest lived.
14:54: ὁ Πέτρος ἀπὸ μακρόθεν ἠκολούθησεν αὐτῷ, ἕως
Here Mark implies that Peter followed from a distance because he did not want anyone to see him and arrest him too.
Here, the word officers refers to servants and attendants in general.
14:55: Here Mark means that the chief priests and the Sanhedrin were trying find evidence against Jesus. In other words, they needed to find people who were willing to say that Jesus had done something very wrong.
Here Mark implies that the chief priests and the Sanhedrin want to convince the Roman authorities to kill Jesus.
14:56: Here Mark implies that, because what the people were testifying about was not the same, the Jewish leaders could use the testimony as evidence to convict Jesus.
14:57: In Jesus’ culture, people would stand up when they were about to give official testimony.
14:58: Here, the word hands refers to main part of the body that people use to make things. So the phrase refers to the whole person who makes things.
Here, the phrase in three days refers to a time period made up of three days.
Here, the phrase made without hands implies that God, not humans, will make this temple.
14:59: Here, just as in 14:56, Mark implies that, because what the people were testifying about was not the same, the Jewish leaders could use the testimony as evidence to convict Jesus.
14:60: In Jesus’ culture, people would stand up when they were about to make an official statement.
Here the high priest is asking Jesus how he will defend himself against the people who have accused him of saying and doing wrong things.
14:61: ὁ … ἐσιώπα, καὶ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνατο οὐδέν
The phrases was silent and did not answer anything mean similar things. Mark is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, the title the Blessed One is a polite way of referring to God.
The word Son is an important title for Jesus, the Son of God.
14:62: When someone sits at the right hand, it symbolizes that person’s honor, authority, and ability to rule.
Here, the phrase at the right hand refers to the place next to a person’s right hand, which would be the “right side.” In the Jesus’ culture, this side was associated with honor or authority.

Here, the word power could refer to: (1) the power that a person sitting at the right hand has. In this case, Jesus implies that the right hand is God’s; (2) God the Father by reference to the power that he has.
14:63: In Jesus’ culture the act of tearing one’s clothing was a symbolic act done to show outrage or grief.
The high priest is using the question form to emphatically state that he thinks that they do not need more witnesses.
Here the high priest implies that they do not need more witnesses to prove that Jesus had done something wrong.
14:64: Here the high priest is asking the rest of the Jewish council to state whether they think Jesus is guilty or innocent and what they should do with him.
14:65: In Jesus’ culture, people would spit on someone to insult that person.
To blindfold someone means to tie a thick cloth around the middle of a person’s head to cover the eyes and prevent that person from seeing.

The guards did not believe that Jesus was a real prophet and could Prophesy. When they demanded that Jesus should Prophesy, they were challenging him to do something they believed he could not do. They were only asking Jesus to Prophesy in order to mock him.
Here the people telling Jesus to Prophesy are implying that they want him to identify who it was who had just hit him. Since he was blindfolded, this would be prophesying.
Here, the word officers refers to servants and attendants in general.
Here Mark implies that the officers took charge of Jesus.
14:66: Here Mark implies that the room where the Sanhedrin was meeting was above the ground. The room could have been raised slightly above the ground above another room.
14:67: Here Mark implies that Peter was still warming himself by the fire in the courtyard of the high priest’s house (see 14:54).
καὶ σὺ μετὰ τοῦ Ναζαρηνοῦ ἦσθα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ
Here the servant girl means that Peter was a disciple of Jesus.
14:68: Here Mark implies that Peter denied that he was with Jesus as his disciple.
οὔτε οἶδα, οὔτε ἐπίσταμαι σὺ τί λέγεις
Here Peter means that servant girl’s words do not apply to him. He does not mean that he was unable to know or understand what the servant girl said.
οὔτε οἶδα, οὔτε ἐπίσταμαι σὺ τί λέγεις
The phrase Neither have I known and the phrase nor do I understand mean basically the same thing. Peter is using the repetition for emphasis.
A forecourt is an open area that leads into another open area (the “court”), which is more closely connected to the house.
Many ancient manuscripts do not include any more words in this verse after the phrase the forecourt. Other ancient manuscripts include the words “and a rooster crowed” after the forecourt.
14:69: Here the servant girl means that Peter was one of the people who traveled with Jesus and were part of his group.
14:70: Here Mark implies that Peter was denying that he was with Jesus as his disciple.
Here the people mean that Peter was one of the people who traveled with Jesus and were part of his group.
The pronoun them refers to Jesus and his disciples.
Here the people standing around imply that, since Peter was a Galilean, he must have been with Jesus, who also was a Galilean.
14:71: Here, the phrase to curse could mean that: (1) Peter asks God to curse him if he is lying; (2) Peter curses Jesus.
14:72: Here, word represents what Jesus just said using words.
πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι δὶς, τρίς με ἀπαρνήσῃ
This clause is basically identical to what Jesus said in 14:30, so express the idea as you did there.

The word translated as having broken down could indicate that: (1) Peter became overwhelmed with grief and lost control of his emotions; (2) Peter was thinking about what had happened; (3) Peter fell down on the ground because of how upset he was; (4) Peter began to weep.
15:1: Here, the phrase having made counsel indicates that the Jewish leaders were working together to figure something out.
Here Mark is referring to the rest of the Sanhedrin. He does not mean that the chief priests, elders, and scribes whom he has previously mentioned were not part of the Sanhedrin.
Here Mark implies that the Jewish council commanded guards to bind Jesus.
Here Mark implies that the Jewish council led Jesus away from the high priest’s house and to the place where Pilate was staying.
Here Mark implies that the Jewish leaders brought Jesus to Pilate because they wanted Pilate to judge him.
15:2: Together the two words answering and says mean that Jesus responded to what Pilate asked him.

Here, the phrase You say {it} indicates that the speaker acknowledges the truth of what the other person said. Jesus uses this phrase to indirectly indicate that Pilate is right to suggest that Jesus is the King of the Jews.
15:3: Here the word translated as of many things could: (1) indicate that the chief priests accused Jesus of doing many different things; (2) indicate that the chief priests accused Jesus many times.
15:4: Here Pilate uses the word See to refer to hearing or paying attention to something.
15:6: Here Mark provides background information about something that Pilate, the governor, normally did. This background information will help readers understand what happens next.
Here, the phrase the festival refers to the Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread, as indicated in 14:1.
Here Mark implies that Pilate normally or customarily did this.
15:7: Here, the word Now marks a continuation of the break in the main story line which began in the preceding verse. Mark is introducing more background information, this time about Barabbas, to help readers understand what happens next.
Here Mark refers to an insurrection that his readers were familiar with. Most likely, this insurrection occurred soon before this story.
15:8: Here Mark indicates that the crowd walked up to where Pilate was. Most likely, this place was on top of a hill in the city of Jerusalem.
Some ancient manuscripts read having come up.
Here Mark implies that the crowd asked Pilate to release a prisoner, just as he usually did.
Here Mark refers to what Pilate normally or customarily did.
15:9: Here Pilate uses the same title for Jesus that he used in 15:2. He does not indicate whether he thinks that Jesus really is the King of the Jews, but he uses the title because Jesus apparently accepted it in 15:2.
15:11: Mark speaks of the chief priests as if they had stirred a pot and put into motion things that had been lying quietly on the bottom. Mark means that the chief priests encouraged the crowd to ask Pilate to release Barabbas.
Here Mark implies that the crowd would ask or demand that Pilate release Barabbas.
Here Mark implies that they asked for Barabbas instead of Jesus.
15:12: ὁ … Πειλᾶτος πάλιν ἀποκριθεὶς ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς
Together the two terms answering and was saying mean that Pilate was responding to what the crowd asked for.
Mark uses the word again here because Pilate had already spoken to them regarding this matter in 15:9.
Here, the word therefore indicates that Pilate asks this question in response to the crowd, who were asking that he release Barabbas.
Many ancient manuscripts read {with the one} you call.
15:13: Here, the word again could indicate: (1) that the crowd had already cried out for Pilate to release Barabbas, as Mark implies in 15:11.
Here the crowd means that they want Pilate to command his soldiers to Crucify him.
15:14: Pilate is using the question form to emphasize that he thinks that Jesus has not done any evil.
15:15: Here Mark implies that Pilate handed Jesus over to his soldiers.
Here Mark implies that Pilate had his soldiers flog Jesus.
Flogging was a Roman penalty in which soldiers whipped a person with a whip to which were attached pieces of bone and metal to increase the whip’s capacity to do harm to the person being flogged.
15:16: τῆς αὐλῆς, ὅ ἐστιν πραιτώριον, καὶ
Here Mark provides an explanation of what this specific courtyard was. Use a form that shows that Mark is giving more information about the courtyard.
Here, the word translated as courtyard could refer to: (1) the open area that was part of the Praetorium; (2) Pilate’s palace or residence.
The Praetorium was where the Roman governor stayed when he was in Jerusalem and where the soldiers in Jerusalem lived.
The word cohort is a military term. Each cohort is a group of about 600 soldiers, which is a tenth of a legion. Most likely, Mark is referring to all the soldiers who were stationed in Jerusalem.
15:17: In Roman culture, a purple robe was like the expensive clothing worn by kings, and in that culture a king usually wore a crown. The soldiers put a purple robe and a crown of thorns on Jesus to pretend that he was a king, even though they did not think that he really was a king. They did this to mock him.
As 15:20 indicates, the soldiers took Jesus’ own clothes off before putting the purple robe on him.
The word purple refers to a color that is a combination of blue and red.
Mark uses the word thorns to refer to small branches with thorns on them.
15:18: Here the soldiers mock Jesus by greeting him as if he were King of the Jews when they do not believe that he actually is. They actually meant to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of their words.
In Jesus’ culture, people commonly greeted each other with the word Rejoice.
15:19: In Jesus’ culture, people would spit on someone to insult that person.

In Jesus’ culture, bending the knee and bowing before someone was a way to respect a greater person, especially when asking the greater person to do a favor. Here, the soldiers perform this action to mock Jesus by pretending that he is a king.
The phrases bending the knee and bowing down mean similar things. Mark is using the two terms together for emphasis.
15:20: Here Mark implies that the soldiers led Jesus out from the Praetorium.
15:21: According to Roman law, Roman soldiers could press someone into service, which means that they could force a person to carry a load for them or work for them. In this case, they forced Simon to carry Jesus’ cross.
The words Simon, Alexander, and Rufus are the names of men.
Κυρηναῖον … τὸν πατέρα Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Ῥούφου
The phrases a Cyrenean and the father of Alexander and Rufus include background information about the man whom the soldiers forced to carry Jesus’ cross.
Here Mark implies that Simon was coming from the farmlands outside Jerusalem and going toward Jerusalem.
15:22: The word Golgotha is an Aramaic word. Mark has spelled it out using Greek letters so his readers would know how it sounded.
15:23: The word myrrh refers to a fragrant resin or gum that is collected from trees.
15:24: Here Mark means that the soldiers took the clothes that Jesus had been wearing and divided them up by giving each piece of clothing to a soldier.

The term lot refers to an object with different markings on various sides that was used to decide randomly among several possibilities. It would be tossed onto the ground to see which marked side would come up on top.
Here Mark implies that this is the purpose for which they were casting a lot.
15:25: Mark uses the word Now to introduce background information, which is the time of day when Jesus was crucified.
In this culture, people began counting the hours each day beginning around daybreak at six o’clock in the morning. So, the third hour would be around nine o’clock in the morning.
15:26: Here, the word inscription refers to a few words written to identify something.

Here the soldiers continue mock Jesus by referring to him as if he were King of the Jews when they do not believe that he actually is. They actually mean to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of their words.
15:28: The notes below discuss translation issues in this verse, for those who decide to include it.
15:29: The people’s action of wagging their heads at Jesus showed that they felt disdain for him and that they disapproved of him.
Here the people refer to Jesus by what the false witnesses testified during his trial that he had said (see 14:58).
Here, the phrase in three days refers to a time period made up of three days.
15:31: In context, the Jewish leaders are implicitly referring to how Jesus saved others by healing their diseases, releasing them from demon-possession, and saving them from other physical problems.
15:32: Here the Jewish leaders use what they think is an imaginary situation to prove that Jesus is not really the Christ, the King of Israel.
ὁ Χριστὸς, ὁ Βασιλεὺς Ἰσραὴλ καταβάτω

Here the Jewish leaders mock Jesus by speaking about him as if he were the Christ, the King of Israel when they do not believe that he actually is. They actually mean to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of their words, as Mark indicated when he says that they mocked Jesus (see 15:31).
Here the Jewish leaders imply that they might see Jesus coming down from the cross and then they might believe that he really is the Christ, the King of Israel.
15:33: In this culture, people began counting the hours each day beginning around daybreak at six o’clock in the morning. So, the sixth hour would be around noon, and the ninth hour would be around three o’clock in the afternoon.
Here, the whole land could refer to: (1) the entire area around where Jesus was crucified. This could include just the city of Jerusalem or all of Palestine; (2) the entire earth.
15:34: Here, the phrase cried out with a loud voice means that Jesus raised the volume of his voice.
This phrase is what Jesus cried out in his own language, either Aramaic or Hebrew. Mark has spelled the words out using Greek letters so his readers would know how they sounded.
See the discussion of this phrase in the chapter introduction.
15:35: Mark implies that the people did not understand what Jesus said. They heard him say “Eloi,” which means “My God,” but they thought it sounded like the name Elijah.
15:36: A sponge is a soft, porous object that can soak up and hold liquid, which comes out of it when the sponge is squeezed.
Here, vinegar refers to the inexpensive and sour wine that common people in Jesus’ culture would usually drink.
The person put the sponge on a reed, or long stick, so that he could hold the sponge up to Jesus.
Here, the clause Leave {him} means that no one should do anything more to or for Jesus.
Here the man implies that Elijah might take him down from the cross.
15:37: Here, the phrase having let out a loud voice means that Jesus shouted loudly.
Mark is referring to death in a polite way by using the word expired.
15:38: Here Mark could be referring to the curtain: (1) that separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; (2) that separated the Holy Place from the rest of the temple area.
15:39: Here, a place opposite him is directly in front of Jesus.
Some ancient manuscripts read he expired in this way.
Son of God is an important title for Jesus that describes his relationship with God the Father.
15:40: Mark uses the word Now to introduce background information that will help readers understand what happens later in the story. The word does not introduce the next event in the story.
The word Mary is the name of a woman. This Mary was not Mary Magdalene nor Mary the mother of Jesus. Mark identifies her instead as the mother of James the younger and of Joses.

The word James is the name of a man. This James is not James the brother of Jesus, James son of Zebedee, or James son of Alphaeus. The word Joses is also the name of a man. This Joses is not Jesus’ brother.

When Mark refers to James as the little, he could mean that: (1) he was younger than one or more other people named James; (2) he was less well-known than one or more other people named James; (3) he was a short man.
15:41: Mark uses the statement who, when he was in Galilee, were following him and serving him to give his readers background information about the relationship that the three women mentioned in 15:40 had with Jesus.
Here, the phrase were following him indicates that these three women had traveled with Jesus and were his disciple.
15:42: Here Mark indicates that Joseph of Arimathea acted as he did (see 15:43) because it was the Day of Preparation. Mark assumes that his readers will know that Jews would not move or bury a body on the Sabbath (the next day). He also assumes that his readers will know that the law includes a command to bury on the same day anyone who was executed as Jesus was (see Deuteronomy 21:22–23). So, if he wanted bury Jesus’ body, Joseph needed to receive the body and bury it quickly, before the next day began.
Here, as Mark indicates the Day of Preparation is the day before the Sabbath. On this day, Jews would prepare for the Sabbath so that they would not have to do work on that day.
15:43: The word Joseph is the name of a man, and the word Arimathea is the name of the city he was from.
Mark uses the word himself to emphasize that Joseph was one of the people who was waiting for the kingdom of God.
The reason that Joseph asked Pilate for the body of Jesus was so that he could bury it.
15:44: Here Mark means that Pilate was not sure whether Jesus had already died, but he marveled that it might be true.
Here Mark implies that this is the same centurion who was in charge of crucifying Jesus (see 15:39).
15:45: Here Mark implies that Pilate learned that Jesus really was dead.
Here Mark implies that Pilate commanded his soldiers to give the corpse to Joseph.
15:46: The term linen cloth refers to a high-quality cloth made from the fibers of the flax plant.

Here Mark implies that other people helped Joseph when he took Jesus’ body down from the cross, prepared it for the tomb, laid it in the tomb, and rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb in order to close it.
Here Mark implies that Joseph took Jesus’ body down from the cross.
This was the burial custom in this culture.
Here Mark means specifically a burial place that had been cut or chiseled out of rock, most likely into the face of a cliff.
προσεκύλισεν λίθον ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν τοῦ μνημείου
Here Mark implies that Joseph rolled the stone to close up the tomb.
15:47: The word Mary is the name of a woman, the same woman whom Mark referred to in 15:40. This Mary was not Mary Magdalene nor Mary the mother of Jesus. Mark identifies her instead as the {mother} of Joses.
The word Joses is also the name of a man, the same man whom Mark referred to in 15:40. This Joses is not Jesus’ brother.
16:1: Here Mark indicates that the sun had set on Saturday, which meant that the Sabbath had ended. The three women were now permitted to do work, like buying spices.

The word Mary is the name of a woman, the same woman whom Mark referred to in 15:40 and 15:47. This Mary was not Mary Magdalene nor Mary the mother of Jesus. Mark identifies her instead as the {mother} of James.
The word James is the name of a man, the same man whom Mark referred to in 15:40. This James is not James the brother of Jesus, James son of Zebedee, or James son of Alphaeus.
The word Salome is the name of a woman. She is the same woman whom Mark referred to in 15:40.

Here, the word spices refers to any good-smelling herbs, ointments, and oils. In Jesus’ culture, it was customary to put these good-smelling things on dead bodies to cover up bad smells and to honor the people who had died. Since the women plan to anoint Jesus with these spices, the spices must be herbs mixed with oil or some kind of ointment.

In Jesus’ culture, it was customary for people to anoint dead bodies when they were buried. Joseph of Arimathea had not done this because he had to bury Jesus quickly before the Sabbath began. These three women now plan to finish the customary burial preparations.
16:2: λείαν πρωῒ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων
Here Mark refers to sunrise on the first of the week, that is, Sunday.
Mark is using the adjective first as a noun to mean the first day.
Here, the phrase the sun having come up refers to sunrise.
16:3: Here Mark implies that they were saying this while they were going to the tomb.
16:5: Here Mark is referring to the right side of the tomb from the women’s perspective.
16:6: Here, the word raised refers to someone who died coming back to life.
Here the young man refers to the place within the tomb where Joseph of Arimathea and his helpers put Jesus’ body. This place was probably a shelf or ledge.
16:7: τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ τῷ Πέτρῳ

The phrase and to Peter is not making a distinction between Peter and the disciples by indicating that Peter is not part of the group of Jesus’ disciples. Rather, the phrase and Peter is being used to emphasize that of all of the disciples of Jesus, these women should take special care to tell Peter the information that follows this phrase.
16:8: Here, when trembling and amazement are gripping people, it means that these people are overcome by trembling and amazement. In other words, they cannot help but experience these things.
Here Mark implies that the women were trembling because of their amazement.
